chunks: Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abdul Rahman ibn Al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) broke his fast on the evening of Thursday in the Mosque of Quba, so he said: 'Is there any drink?' So Aws ibn Khawlan al-Ansari brought him a vessel of buttermilk with honey.

So when he placed it near his mouth, he set it aside, then said: 'Two drinks, one can suffice from the other. I neither drink it nor do I prohibit it, but I am being humble to Allah. For whoever is humble to Allah, Allah elevates him; and whoever is arrogant, Allah lowers him; and whoever is economical in his livelihood, Allah provides for him; and whoever is a spendthrift, Allah deprives him; and whoever frequently remembers death, Allah loves him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the Prophet setting aside buttermilk and honey, and what ethical lessons are derived from this act?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, the Prophet (SAWW) demonstrates *tawaduu'* (humility) by setting aside a drink of buttermilk and honey not due to *haram* or lack of need, but to elevate his spiritual status before Allah. This incident highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on voluntary modesty as a means of divine elevation, linking it practically to economic moderation (*iqtisad*) and constant awareness of death (*dhikr al-mawt*).

en.hubeali:
Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Abdul Rahman Bin Al Hajjaj, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup style="font-weight: normal">asws</sup> having said:

‘Rasool-Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> broke his<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> Fast in the evening of Thursday in Masjid Quba. So he<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> said: ‘Is there anything to drink?’ So Aws Bin Howly came to him<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> with some buttermilk with honey.

So when he<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> placed it upon his<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> mouth, set it aside, then said: ‘Two drinks, one can be sufficed from its counterpart. I<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> neither drink it nor do I<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> prohibit it, but I<sup style="font-weight: normal">saww</sup> am being humble to Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">azwj</sup>, for the one who is humble to Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">azwj</sup>, Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">azwj</sup> would Elevate him, and the one who is arrogant, Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">azwj</sup> would Downgrade him; and the one who is economical in his life, Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">azwj</sup> would Grace him; and the one who is a spendthrift, Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">azwj</sup> would Deprive him; and the one who is frequent in remembering the death, Allah<sup style="font-weight: normal">azwj</sup> would Love him’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ibn abu ‘Umayr has narrated from ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) who has said the following:

‘‘In a Thursday evening the Messenger of Allah had completed his day’s fasting and dinner was served in the Mosque of Quba. He asked, ‘Is there any drink?’ Aws ibn Khuli brought him a bowl of milk mixed with honey.

When he touched it with his lips he moved it away saying, ‘There are two drinks each of which is enough drink. I will not drink it and I am not making unlawful to drink it, but I want to be humble before Allah. Whoever is humble before Allah, He raises him up, and whoever is arrogant, Allah brings him low. Whoever economizes in his living Allah grants him sustenance. Whoever is a spendthrift, Allah deprives him. Whoever speaks of death very often, Allah loves him.’”
